Name: Saga
Problem: Need atomic business transaction across multiple services without distributed 2PC
Solution: Decompose into a sequence of local transactions; each step has a compensating action invoked on failure (orchestration or choreography)
When to Use: Long-running cross-service workflows (order, payment, fulfilment); polyglot persistence
When NOT to Use: Single-DB transactions, hard real-time invariants requiring strong consistency
Trade-offs: Eventual consistency, complex compensation logic, must design for retries & idempotency
Related Patterns: Outbox, CQRS, Event Sourcing, Process Manager
Keywords: saga compensating transaction orchestration choreography microservice

Name: CQRS
Problem: Same data model is forced to serve very different read/write workloads
Solution: Split into separate Command and Query models, possibly with different storage and projections
When to Use: High read/write asymmetry, complex domain, audit needs, polyglot persistence
When NOT to Use: Simple CRUD apps with low scale; when team can't operate two models
Trade-offs: Eventual consistency between write & read sides; operational complexity
Keywords: cqrs command query separation read model write model

Name: Event Sourcing
Problem: Need full audit trail and ability to reconstruct state at any point in time
Solution: Persist every state change as an immutable event; current state is a fold over events
When to Use: Audit/regulatory needs, complex domain, temporal queries, debugging via replay
When NOT to Use: Simple CRUD; teams new to DDD; very high write throughput where event store is bottleneck
Trade-offs: Schema evolution is hard, snapshots required for performance, eventual consistency on projections
Keywords: event sourcing append-only event store projection snapshot

Name: Transactional Outbox
Problem: Need to atomically persist a row AND publish a message without 2PC
Solution: Write the message to an 'outbox' table in the same DB transaction; a relay process forwards to the broker
When to Use: Ensuring at-least-once event publishing for state changes
When NOT to Use: When using a broker that supports transactions with the DB (rare); for fire-and-forget non-critical events
Trade-offs: Adds relay process & duplicate-delivery handling; small write amplification
Keywords: outbox cdc debezium event publish atomic

Name: Change Data Capture (CDC)
Problem: Need a reliable stream of database changes for downstream systems
Solution: Tail the DB transaction log (WAL/binlog/oplog) and publish change events to a stream
When to Use: Replicating to data warehouse, search index hydration, event-driven side effects, zero-downtime migrations
When NOT to Use: High-velocity OLTP where WAL pressure becomes a bottleneck without tuning
Trade-offs: Schema changes need careful rollout; ordering & exactly-once require care
Keywords: cdc debezium binlog wal logical replication kafka connect

Name: Circuit Breaker
Problem: A failing downstream dependency cascades failures and exhausts callers' threads/connections
Solution: Wrap remote calls in a state machine (closed/open/half-open) that fails fast when error rate exceeds threshold
When to Use: Synchronous calls to potentially unhealthy services; protecting tail latency
When NOT to Use: Calls inside a single trusted process; non-idempotent calls without retry budget
Trade-offs: Adds latency overhead and tuning surface (thresholds, windows, timeouts)
Keywords: circuit breaker hystrix resilience4j fail-fast cascading failure

Name: Bulkhead
Problem: One slow tenant/dependency exhausts a shared thread/connection pool and starves others
Solution: Partition resources (thread pools, connection pools, queues) per tenant or downstream so one bad actor cannot sink the whole service
When to Use: Multi-tenant gateways, services calling many heterogeneous backends
When NOT to Use: Single-tenant low-traffic services where partitioning costs > benefit
Trade-offs: Lower utilisation; more pools to size & monitor
Keywords: bulkhead isolation thread pool resource partition tenant

Name: Retry with Exponential Backoff + Jitter
Problem: Transient failures cause unnecessary user-visible errors; naive retries cause thundering herd
Solution: Retry with exponentially increasing delay and randomised jitter; cap attempts and total budget
When to Use: Idempotent network calls (GET/PUT/DELETE), broker publishes, DB queries
When NOT to Use: Non-idempotent operations without idempotency keys; user-facing flows where speed matters more
Trade-offs: More latency on failure; can amplify load if budgets misconfigured
Related Patterns: Circuit Breaker, Idempotent Receiver, Token Bucket
Keywords: retry exponential backoff jitter thundering herd idempotent

Name: Idempotency Key
Problem: At-least-once delivery causes duplicate side effects (double charges, double creates)
Solution: Caller supplies an opaque key; server stores result keyed by it and replays the response on duplicate requests
When to Use: Payments, order creation, any non-GET operation in distributed/eventual systems
When NOT to Use: Truly read-only or naturally idempotent operations
Trade-offs: Storage cost & TTL management; key collision design
Keywords: idempotency key duplicate exactly once at-least-once

Name: Leader Election
Problem: Need exactly one instance to perform a singleton task in a horizontally scaled deployment
Solution: Use a consensus-backed lock (Raft/ZAB) or atomic lease in etcd/ZooKeeper/Redis (Redlock with caveats)
When to Use: Distributed cron, partition assignment, primary failover
When NOT to Use: When the task can be safely sharded or run on every replica
Trade-offs: Split-brain risk if lease/lease-renewal misconfigured; added dependency
Keywords: leader election lease lock raft zookeeper etcd consul

Name: Sidecar
Problem: Cross-cutting concerns (TLS, observability, traffic shaping) repeated in every service
Solution: Run a co-located helper container alongside the app sharing network/lifecycle (e.g. Envoy, OTel collector)
When to Use: Service mesh, log/metric shipping, secret renewal
When NOT to Use: Hot paths where extra hop's latency matters; resource-constrained edges
Trade-offs: Per-pod overhead, additional release surface
Keywords: sidecar envoy istio linkerd otel collector mesh

Name: Strangler Fig
Problem: Need to incrementally replace a legacy system without big-bang rewrite
Solution: Front the legacy with a router; carve off and re-implement capabilities one at a time, retiring legacy slices
When to Use: Brownfield modernisation, monolith-to-microservices
When NOT to Use: Greenfield projects; when carve-out boundaries aren't yet stable
Trade-offs: Long migration period with two systems; routing complexity
Keywords: strangler fig migration legacy monolith decomposition

Name: Anti-Corruption Layer
Problem: Integration with legacy or external system would pollute domain model
Solution: Translate between models at the boundary; keep your domain pure
When to Use: DDD bounded-context integration, third-party SaaS adapters
When NOT to Use: Tiny adapters where translation is trivial
Trade-offs: Extra layer to maintain; potential perf cost
Keywords: anti-corruption layer ddd bounded context translation

Name: Backend for Frontend (BFF)
Problem: Different clients (web/mobile/IoT) need different aggregations and shapes from the same backend
Solution: One BFF per client type that aggregates and tailors responses
When to Use: Polyglot client portfolio with divergent needs
When NOT to Use: Single client; bandwidth-cheap simple APIs
Trade-offs: Duplicates aggregation logic across BFFs; potential N+1 to backends
Keywords: bff backend for frontend api gateway aggregation

Name: API Gateway
Problem: Many internal services should not be exposed individually to clients
Solution: Single ingress that handles auth, rate-limit, routing, transformation, observability
When to Use: Edge of microservices, multi-tenant SaaS
When NOT to Use: Single small service; gRPC mesh-internal traffic
Trade-offs: Single point of contention; deployment coupling risk
Keywords: api gateway kong krakend envoy ingress edge

Name: Rate Limiting / Throttling
Problem: Protect downstreams and ensure fair use among tenants
Solution: Token bucket / leaky bucket / sliding window enforced at gateway, service, or per-route
When to Use: Public APIs, multi-tenant SaaS, abuse protection
When NOT to Use: Internal trusted RPC with stable load
Trade-offs: Tuning per tier; clock skew issues with distributed counters
Keywords: rate limit token bucket leaky bucket throttle quota

Name: Sharding
Problem: Single dataset/store cannot meet capacity or latency requirements
Solution: Partition data by a key (hash, range, geo) across nodes; route requests by partition
When to Use: Multi-tenant data, time-series, very large OLTP
When NOT to Use: Sub-TB datasets fitting comfortably in a single node
Trade-offs: Cross-shard joins/transactions are painful; rebalancing is non-trivial
Keywords: shard partition consistent hashing resharding

Name: Read Replica
Problem: Read-heavy workload saturates the primary
Solution: Replicate primary asynchronously to N read-only replicas; route reads via load balancer
When to Use: BI/dashboards, search, anything tolerant of lag
When NOT to Use: Strict read-after-write workloads without read-your-writes routing
Trade-offs: Replica lag visibility; stale reads
Keywords: read replica replication async lag failover

Name: Materialized View
Problem: Expensive aggregation/join is repeated on every read
Solution: Precompute and store the result; refresh on event or schedule
When to Use: Dashboards, leaderboards, search-style queries
When NOT to Use: Highly volatile data with no query reuse
Trade-offs: Stale data window; refresh cost & invalidation
Keywords: materialized view projection precompute aggregate

Name: Process Manager / Orchestrator
Problem: Long-running multi-step process needs explicit state, timers, and recovery
Solution: Use a workflow engine (Temporal, Cadence, Step Functions, Camunda) to model state machines/durable executions
When to Use: Order fulfilment, KYC, ETL pipelines, human-in-the-loop
When NOT to Use: Simple stateless request/response
Trade-offs: Vendor lock-in; engine becomes critical infra; debugging requires tooling
Keywords: temporal cadence camunda step functions durable workflow

Name: Outbox + Inbox
Problem: Both atomic publish and idempotent consumption are needed for exactly-once-effect
Solution: Producer uses Outbox; consumer uses Inbox table to deduplicate by message id
When to Use: Critical financial/state-changing events
When NOT to Use: Pure analytics streams where duplicates are tolerable
Trade-offs: Storage overhead; need TTL or compaction on inbox
Keywords: outbox inbox dedup exactly-once idempotent consumer

Name: Fan-Out / Scatter-Gather
Problem: A request needs results from many backends with bounded latency
Solution: Issue calls in parallel, optionally with hedged requests; aggregate within a deadline
When to Use: Search aggregation, recommendation, federated queries
When NOT to Use: Strict serial dependencies; cost-sensitive backends
Trade-offs: Tail-latency dominated by slowest dependency unless hedged
Source URL: Google SRE: 'The Tail at Scale' (Dean & Barroso)
Keywords: scatter gather fan-out hedged request federated
